label: Temptation
framing: Temptation itself is not sin, Jesus was tempted in every way and did not fall. Scripture treats it not as a private shame to hide but as a real battle to fight, and it promises that no temptation comes without a way out, if you will take it.
cultural: The wilderness account shows Jesus tempted at the points where every human breaks, appetite, power, and the demand that God prove himself, and answering each with Scripture rather than willpower. His world, like ours, knew that desire is strong and the flesh is weak, and the Bible never pretends the pull is small, only that it can be resisted.
historical: The desert fathers of the fourth century mapped how a tempting thought grows from a suggestion to a foothold to a habit, and taught believers to cut it off early, before it took root. The long tradition of confession and accountability rests on a hard-won truth, that sin fought in secret almost always wins, and sin brought into the light begins to lose its grip.
application: Fight temptation upstream, before the moment of heat, by removing what feeds it and planning your escape in advance. Refuse to fight alone, name the struggle to a trusted friend, since secrecy is the addiction's oxygen. Flee rather than negotiate, as Joseph did, and if a habit has become a true addiction, get real help and treatment, which is courage and not weakness.

verses.text: When the woman saw that the tree was good for food and pleasing to the eyes, and that it was desirable for obtaining wisdom, she took the fruit and ate it. She also gave some to her husband who was with her, and he ate it.
verses.where: The first temptation in the Bible. The serpent questions God's word and his goodness, and the fruit looks good, pleasing and desirable. Temptation usually comes dressed as something good, with a doubt about God attached.

verses.text: When tempted, no one should say, “God is tempting me.” For God cannot be tempted by evil, nor does He tempt anyone. But each one is tempted when by his own evil desires he is lured away and enticed. Then after desire has conceived, it gives birth to sin; and sin, when it is full-grown, gives birth to death.
verses.where: James refuses to let anyone blame God for temptation. It grows from a person's own desires, and he traces its path like a birth: desire conceives, gives birth to sin, and sin grown up brings death. The earlier it is stopped, the better.

verses.text: Then Jesus was led by the Spirit into the wilderness to be tempted by the devil.
verses.where: Right after his baptism, the Spirit leads Jesus into the wilderness, where he fasts and is tempted by the devil. He answers each temptation with Scripture from Deuteronomy. Being tempted is not itself sin; Jesus was tempted.

verses.text: For we do not have a high priest who is unable to sympathize with our weaknesses, but we have one who was tempted in every way that we are, yet was without sin. Let us then approach the throne of grace with confidence, so that we may receive mercy and find grace to help us in our time of need.
verses.where: Jesus is called a high priest who was tempted in every way we are, yet without sin. Because he understands, the tempted can come to God's throne with confidence and find help at the time they need it.

verses.text: For I do not do the good I want to do. Instead, I keep on doing the evil I do not want to do.
verses.where: Paul describes the war between wanting good and doing evil. Interpreters differ on whether he speaks of his life before Christ or as a believer, but readers in every age have recognized themselves here. The passage ends in a cry for rescue and thanks to God through Jesus Christ.

verses.text: “Watch and pray so that you will not enter into temptation. For the spirit is willing, but the body is weak.”
verses.where: In Gethsemane Jesus finds his disciples asleep and warns them to watch and pray so that they will not fall into temptation. He knows their willing spirit and their weak bodies.

verses.text: She grabbed Joseph by his cloak and said, “Sleep with me!” But leaving his cloak in her hand, he escaped and ran outside.
verses.where: Potiphar's wife presses Joseph day after day. When she grabs him, he leaves his cloak in her hand and runs. Sometimes the wise answer to temptation is not to argue with it but to leave.

verses.text: Flee from youthful passions and pursue righteousness, faith, love, and peace, together with those who call on the Lord out of a pure heart.
verses.where: Paul tells Timothy to flee youthful passions and to pursue righteousness, faith, love and peace, together with others who call on the Lord. Fleeing is paired with pursuing, and with company.

verses.text: Therefore confess your sins to each other and pray for each other so that you may be healed. The prayer of a righteous man has great power to prevail.
verses.where: James tells believers to confess their sins to each other and pray for each other. Hidden sin keeps its power; sin brought into the light among people who pray loses some of it.

verses.text: If we confess our sins, He is faithful and just to forgive us our sins and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.
verses.where: John writes to believers who still sin, and warns against pretending otherwise. The answer to falling again is confession, and God's faithfulness to forgive.

misread.taken: This verse is often turned into the saying “God won't give you more than you can handle,” and used about illness, grief or trouble of every kind.
misread.says: Paul is warning the Corinthians about temptation, especially the pull of idolatry, using Israel in the wilderness as the example. The promise is that no temptation is unique, that God is faithful, and that with the temptation he will provide a way out so that you can stand. It promises strength to stand, not a life without testing, and it is not a promise that suffering will never be more than a person can bear. Paul himself wrote of hardship “far beyond our ability to endure” (2 Corinthians 1:8).
misread.text: No temptation has seized you except what is common to man. And God is faithful; He will not let you be tempted beyond what you can bear. But when you are tempted, He will also provide an escape, so that you can stand up under it.

whole: Most people who type “temptation” are not asking about a single moment. They are asking about a pattern: the same sin, the same place, the same promise to stop, the same failure. Shame grows with every round, and shame makes the next round easier, because it pushes the struggle into hiding. Many come to believe they are uniquely weak, or that God must be tired of them.

The Bible is honest about how temptation works. It usually arrives as something good, with a whisper that God is holding out on you. It grows from desire, slowly, and gains strength in secret. And it is common to everyone: Paul says no temptation has seized anyone except what is common to man, and Jesus himself was tempted. Being tempted is not sin. Feeding the desire, hiding it, and telling yourself it is the last time, again, is how it becomes one.

So Scripture's wisdom is both humble and practical. Watch and pray, because the body is weak. Know your patterns and leave early, like Joseph, rather than arguing in the doorway. Do not fight alone: confess to someone you trust and let them pray with you. When you fall, do not hide; confess to God, who is faithful to forgive, and get up. And remember the high priest who was tempted and did not sin, who understands, and before whom you can come with confidence. Change often comes slowly, but it comes, and the way out God promises is real.

differ.share: Christians agree that temptation is not sin, that God gives strength and a way out, that confession and forgiveness are for believers who fall, and that the struggle is a real part of the Christian life.

views.name: Paul as a believer
views.body: Many in the tradition of Augustine and the Reformers read Romans 7:14-25 as Paul's own struggle as a Christian, a war that continues until the life to come.

views.name: Life under the law
views.body: Many early Greek interpreters, and many scholars today, read the passage as describing life under the law without the Spirit, with Romans 8 showing the freedom of life in the Spirit that follows.

differ.after: Both read Romans 8 as the answer: there is no condemnation for those in Christ Jesus, and the Spirit gives life.

deep.sit: Where and when does this temptation usually find you, and what would it look like to leave that place earlier this week?

prayer.lead: Psalm 51 is the prayer of someone who fell badly. These lines ask God for a new heart, not just another resolution.
prayer.text: Create in me a clean heart, O God, and renew a right spirit within me. Cast me not away from Your presence; take not Your Holy Spirit from me. Restore to me the joy of Your salvation, and sustain me with a willing spirit.
